directions.title: Philosophy and vision
paragraphs: I treat self-assembly as a design problem: start from a target structure and encode it in the interactions between DNA building blocks.

Longer term, I want to move from structure to function: positioning functional components and carrying DNA-designed geometry into durable materials with optical and transport properties. I also see AI tools, working with simulation and experiment, shortening the design–build–test cycle toward automated laboratory workflows.

methods.title: Methods and workflow
paragraphs: A design is first tested in coarse-grained simulation to find the competing structures that could also form, then built and characterized in the lab; each experiment feeds back into the next model.

groups.label: Open crystal lattices
groups.title: Selecting crystal topology by interaction design
groups.description: Computationally designed interactions select the topology of DNA-origami crystals, with structures verified by scattering and microscopy.

groups.label: Finite 3D assemblies
groups.title: Designing objects from programmable cubes
groups.description: DNA-origami cubes carry designed interaction rules that direct them into finite 3D objects and extended lattices. Inverse design selects the intended structures while accounting for competing assemblies.

groups.label: Lattice selection
groups.title: One building block, three lattices
groups.description: One tetrahedral building block forms cubic diamond, hexagonal diamond, or ice 0 when only its four sticky ends change. Calculations on idealized high-refractive-index versions of these lattices explore their photonic potential.

story.title: A hexagonal diamond connection
story.description: Hexagonal diamond: from DNA lattices to Meteor Crater
paragraphs: In 1967, a hexagonal polymorph of diamond was described in shock-transformed graphite inclusions from the Canyon Diablo iron meteorite, the body that formed Arizona’s Meteor Crater. Whether those grains are a distinct hexagonal phase or stacking-disordered cubic diamond has been debated, and the interpretation refined, ever since.

I visited the crater after leading a study that reports selective assembly of the same diamond network at the colloidal scale. The shared problem is polytype selection, not composition: cubic and hexagonal diamond differ only in stacking sequence, which is exactly what makes it hard to show that one has formed rather than the other. The meteoritic case is a long-running example of that difficulty in shock-transformed carbon; the laboratory crystal is assembled from DNA-origami tetrahedra, where the stacking is set by design and read out by scattering.

foundations.title: Molecular programming foundations
paragraphs: Work on RNA and RNA:DNA strand displacement tested how toehold length, substrate-end placement, and mismatch position affect reaction kinetics. It established an experimental foundation for reasoning about sequence, dynamics, and off-target behavior.
I also contributed to a localized DNA reaction network that implemented state transitions with temporal resolution.
